result:
The library closed at nine, but the lights in the reading room stayed on a little longer, the way a conversation lingers after the last sentence. Outside, rain threaded the streetlamps into soft gold. Inside, a single chair remained occupied by someone who had not come for any particular book, only for the particular quiet that books make when they are left alone together.

She opened a volume at random and found, on the flyleaf, a note in pencil so faint it might have been a thought that had not yet decided to become handwriting: *If you are reading this, the story has already chosen you.* She smiled, because the sentence was both true and ridiculous, which is the usual condition of most interesting things. Turning the page, she discovered the rest of the book was blank. Not empty—blank, the way a field is blank before weather arrives.

So she began, not with a plot, but with a sound: the soft click of the heating pipes, the distant hush of tires on wet asphalt, the almost-inaudible shift of paper settling under its own weight. She wrote those down. Then she wrote the color of the rainlight on the oak table, which was not quite amber and not quite silver. Then she wrote the name of a street she had never walked, and a bakery on that street that sold bread still warm at midnight, and a person who bought the last loaf and carried it home under their coat so the rain would not cool it.

None of this was required. None of it would be graded or published or even, perhaps, reread. Yet the blank pages accepted every sentence without complaint, and the room seemed to lean a fraction closer, as if listening were a form of weather too. When the lights finally dimmed on their timer, she closed the book gently. The note on the flyleaf had not changed, but the pages after it were no longer blank. They held a small, unrepeatable weather of their own.

She left the book on the table for whoever might find it next. Outside, the rain had thinned to a mist that made every streetlamp look like the beginning of a story someone else would finish.
